prompt: The zone file in the infrastructure repository gains the line `docs   CNAME   docs-host.provider.net`. After the deploy, `docs.example.com` resolves to nothing, and `dig` shows the alias pointing at `docs-host.provider.net.example.com`. What went wrong?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 8.

choices.text: A `CNAME` can only sit at the bare domain, never at a subdomain
choices.why: It is the other way round: the bare domain is the one name that cannot carry a `CNAME`, because its `NS` records sit there.

choices.text: The target has no final dot, so the zone's own name was added to it
choices.why: In a record file a name without a trailing dot is completed with the domain, which is exactly the `.example.com` on the end.

choices.text: The record is still propagating, and resolvers will catch up within two days
choices.why: Nothing propagates, and what `dig` printed is already the wrong name rather than an old answer.

choices.text: `docs` also holds a `TXT` record, and an alias may sit beside nothing else
choices.why: That rule is real, but breaking it would not invent a name ending in `example.com`; a missing dot does.

prompt: The shop's owner lowers a price. A developer reloads the API response with *Disable cache* ticked in the network panel and still sees the old price, and the response carries `X-Cache-Status: HIT`, which the Nginx in front of the application adds. Why did ticking the box not help?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 11; Web Servers and Caching, lesson 5.

choices.text: The browser ignored the box and answered from the copy on its own disk
choices.why: A copy from the browser's disk never reaches Nginx, and the `X-Cache-Status` header shows that this request did.

choices.text: The new price never reached the database, which is what `HIT` reports
choices.why: `HIT` says where Nginx found the answer, not what the database holds; asked past the cache, the application gives the new price.

choices.text: Nginx obeys the box only once `proxy_ignore_headers Cache-Control` is set
choices.why: That line makes Nginx ignore what the application says about caching, and it is the line that turns a cache into a leak.

choices.text: The box rules the browser's copies; Nginx's shared cache takes no orders from clients
choices.why: Nginx ignores what a client asks for by design, so the stale copy is on the server, and that is where it has to be refreshed or removed.

prompt: The checkout's availability SLI is `sum(rate(http_server_requests_total{route="/checkout",code!~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_server_requests_total{route="/checkout"}[5m]))`, and it read 1 all week. Meanwhile twenty customers report that their order was never placed, and the network panel on one of them shows the checkout answered `200` with `{"error": "stock service unavailable"}` in the body. Why did the indicator not move?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6; Observability and Operations, lesson 15.

choices.text: The service reported its failures as successes, and the SLI reads the status code
choices.why: Everything between the service and its caller acts on the number, and this one said success; an SLI that counts every non-`5xx` as good counted these orders as good.

choices.text: The `/health` probe was counted with the checkouts and drowned the failures
choices.why: The expression names `route="/checkout"`, so a probe on another route never entered either sum.

choices.text: They were `4xx` errors caused by the customers, which the SLI rightly counts as good
choices.why: The status line said `200`; the error existed only in the body, where no indicator looks.

choices.text: A five-minute window smooths short bursts of failures down to nothing
choices.why: A ratio over five minutes still falls below 1 when a single checkout in it is counted bad; none of these was.

prompt: A nightly copy from São Paulo to Northern Virginia runs over one TCP connection whose window never grows past 64 kilobytes. Take the round trip at the 76.6 ms floor the cloud course works out for that pair. Reasoning as lesson 3 does about data in flight, about how many megabits per second can that connection carry, whatever the link's bandwidth?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 3; Cloud and Serverless, lesson 9.

prompt: A new virtual server has just come up on a public address, with nothing installed on it yet. Which of these does lesson 9 put in its first hour? Choose all that apply.
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 9.

choices.text: Apply the waiting updates, and arrange for security updates to keep arriving
choices.why: An unpatched machine on a public address is found by automated scanning within hours of going up.

choices.text: Buy a size above what you expect, so the machine never runs short
choices.why: The lesson says to buy small and watch; the headroom worth leaving is memory, which is what small applications run out of first.

choices.text: Turn password logins off and log in with a key
choices.why: The scanning that finds the machine is guessing passwords, and a key makes the guessing pointless rather than slow.

choices.text: Run the application as the administrator, so it can reach whatever it needs
choices.why: A separate account with only the access the application needs turns a compromise into a smaller one.

choices.text: Leave every port open until the application is finished, then close the unused ones
choices.why: The first hour closes everything not in use: a firewall that permits the web ports and your way in, and refuses the rest.

choices.text: Decide the backups while the machine is still empty
choices.why: It takes ten minutes now, and nobody backs up the database unless somebody arranges it.

prompt: A storefront can hold two hundred requests in flight. Its search service becomes slow, though not broken. Put what follows in the order lesson 1 tells it.
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 1.
items: Search starts taking four seconds to answer instead of forty milliseconds
Each request that needs search keeps its slot for those four seconds
All two hundred slots end up held by requests waiting on search
Requests that never touch search find no free slot and cannot get in
Everybody sees an outage while the storefront's own measurements look healthy
trap: Requests that have nothing to do with search are not hurt first: they are turned away only after every slot is already held by one waiting on search.

prompt: The pipeline gives every built asset a hashed name and serves those names for a year. The HTML page that lists them has to be checked with the server on every load, which mostly comes back `304`. Its header is `Cache-Control: ___`.
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 7.

prompt: Your API allows each source address 100 requests a minute and answers `429` after that. A customer says most of their office has been getting `429` all morning, though each person sends only a few requests. What explains it?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 2.

choices.text: Their browsers open several connections each, and the limit counts connections
choices.why: The limit counts requests per address, and the number of connections carrying them changes nothing about that.

choices.text: Their line loses packets, and each TCP retransmission arrives as another request
choices.why: A retransmitted segment is resent below HTTP and handed to the program once; it is never a second request.

choices.text: The office goes out through NAT, so all of its people arrive from one address
choices.why: Every machine in the office appears outside as the router's one public address, which is how a per-address rule shuts out a whole office.

choices.text: Their resolver keeps an old address and sends the whole office to one server
choices.why: Which server answers does not change the address the requests come from, and that address is what the limit counts.

prompt: After a release, every call from the `front` pods to `http://shop` fails at once with `Connection refused`. From a debug pod, `nslookup shop` returns the Service's cluster address, and the `shop` pods are all Running and Ready. Which explanation fits?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 3; Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 15.

choices.text: The Service's selector matches no pod, so its endpoint list is empty
choices.why: A Service with nobody behind it still resolves, and its address refuses connections straight away: the symptom of a typo in the selector's labels.

choices.text: A NetworkPolicy added in the release now drops everything sent to `shop`
choices.why: A drop sends nothing back, so the caller waits until it times out; this refusal came at once.

choices.text: CoreDNS is failing, so `front` cannot turn the name `shop` into an address
choices.why: The name resolved to the cluster address, and a connection can only be refused once an address has been tried.

choices.text: The Service listens on port 80 while the pods use 8080, and the two numbers must match
choices.why: `targetPort` maps one to the other; port 80 on the Service in front of 8080 in the container is the ordinary arrangement.

prompt: The application servers, all Linux, call a partner's API on port 443. Their subnet's network ACL, which is stateless, allows outbound TCP to port 443 and inbound TCP on ports 1024 to 32767, because somebody took that for the ephemeral range. Every call times out. Why?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 2; Cloud and Serverless, lesson 6.

choices.text: The outbound rule has to cover ports 1024 to 65535, since requests leave from them
choices.why: The outbound rule matches the request's destination, 443, which is allowed; the ports that are judged wrongly here are the ones the replies come back to.

choices.text: Linux takes source ports from 32768 to 60999, so every reply lands outside the rule
choices.why: The kernel's `ip_local_port_range` runs from 32768 to 60999, and a stateless filter judges each reply on its own; none of them falls between 1024 and 32767.

choices.text: The instances' security group needs an inbound rule for the replies as well
choices.why: A security group is stateful: the reply to a connection the instance opened comes back in without a rule of its own.

choices.text: The partner's API refuses connections on port 443 from addresses it does not know
choices.why: A refusal comes back at once as `Connection refused`; a timeout means something dropped the packets without a word.

prompt: A new container's `/etc/resolv.conf` says `nameserver 192.0.2.53`, which is `ns1`, the company's authoritative server for `example.com`. Names under `example.com` resolve; every other name fails, and `dig` for one of them shows `status: REFUSED` and `WARNING: recursion requested but not available`. What is wrong?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 4.

choices.text: A firewall blocks port 53 from the container towards the internet
choices.why: A blocked port gives no answer at all, and `dig` would time out; here a server answered.

choices.text: Those names do not exist, and `REFUSED` is how a resolver says so
choices.why: A name that does not exist comes back as `NXDOMAIN`, with the zone's `SOA` in the answer.

choices.text: The authoritative servers of those other domains are down
choices.why: A resolver that tried and failed answers `SERVFAIL`; `REFUSED` means this server would not take the question.

choices.text: It was given a server that answers for its own zones only and never recurses
choices.why: `ns1` holds `example.com` and walks the tree for nobody, which is what the warning says; the container needs a recursive resolver.

prompt: On the monitoring box, CHECK stands for `echo | openssl s_client -connect www.example.com:443 -servername www.example.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -checkend 2592000 >/dev/null`. Which crontab line mails you only once the certificate the site serves has less than thirty days left?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 6; Linux and the Command Line, lesson 13.

choices.text: `0 7 * * * CHECK && echo "www: certificate ends within 30 days"`
choices.why: `&&` runs on exit status 0, which is *will not expire*: a mail every morning while all is well, and silence from the day it matters.

choices.text: `0 7 * * * CHECK || echo "www: certificate ends within 30 days" >/dev/null 2>&1`
choices.why: Cron mails what a job prints, and this line sends the warning to `/dev/null`, so it can never tell anybody anything.

choices.text: `0 7 * * * CHECK || echo "www: certificate ends within 30 days"`
choices.why: `-checkend` exits non-zero when the certificate ends within the 2592000 seconds, `||` runs only then, and cron mails the line `echo` prints.

choices.text: The same line with `-checkend 30` inside CHECK, then `|| echo "www: ends soon"`
choices.why: `-checkend` counts seconds, so 30 warns half a minute before the end; thirty days is `2592000`.

prompt: Before changing DNS, you want to see `https://www.example.com/` exactly as a visitor will once the name points at the new server, 192.0.2.81, which also hosts several other sites. Which command shows it?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 6; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6.

choices.text: `curl --resolve www.example.com:443:192.0.2.81 https://www.example.com/`
choices.why: The name stays in the URL, so it travels in `Host:` and in the handshake and is checked against the certificate; only the address is chosen by hand, without touching DNS.

choices.text: `curl -H 'Host: www.example.com' https://192.0.2.81/`
choices.why: `Host:` picks the right site, but curl checks the certificate against `192.0.2.81` and stops with `no alternative certificate subject name matches`.

choices.text: `curl -k https://192.0.2.81/`, taking whatever certificate it gets
choices.why: With no name in the request the server cannot tell which of its sites you mean, and `-k` switches off the one check that tells a real server from an impostor.

choices.text: `curl https://www.example.com/`, run once DNS points the name at 192.0.2.81
choices.why: That tests after the switch, which is what you set out to avoid; `--resolve` reaches the new address without waiting for DNS.

prompt: A new service on cloud machines sends password-reset mail as `noreply@example.com`, delivering each message straight to the customer's mail server. `example.com` publishes `v=spf1 mx -all` and a DMARC record with `p=reject`. Customers receive nothing. Which fix keeps the domain's policy as it is?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 9.

choices.text: Change `-all` to `~all`, so those machines count only as a soft fail
choices.why: DMARC passes only when SPF or DKIM passes for the `From:` domain; a soft fail is still not a pass, and nothing signed the message.

choices.text: Send through `example.com`'s own server on 587, with a login
choices.why: That server is in the SPF record through `mx` and signs what leaves with DKIM, so both checks pass for `example.com`, and DMARC with them.

choices.text: Have the provider set `PTR` records naming the machines `mail.example.com`
choices.why: A reverse name helps a sender's reputation, but neither SPF nor DKIM reads it, so DMARC fails all the same.

choices.text: Publish `p=none` until the service is finished, then put `p=reject` back
choices.why: That changes the policy, and while it lasts anybody can send as `example.com`; the reset mail still fails both checks.

prompt: Behind a new tunnel to another office, `ping -M do -s 1372` to a server on the far side gets an answer and `ping -M do -s 1373` fails. So that large transfers stop hanging, the router will clamp the MSS of TCP over IPv4 to fit that path. What MSS should it set?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 2.

prompt: A service's calls to an HTTPS API fail with `SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate`. Which of these produce exactly that message? Choose all that apply.
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 6.

choices.text: The certificate's `notAfter` date is already in the past
choices.why: That one is `certificate has expired`, verify code 10.

choices.text: The API's server sends its own certificate without the intermediate
choices.why: The client holds the root and cannot reach it, because the link in the middle was never sent.

choices.text: The certificate names other hosts and not the one in the URL
choices.why: That one is `no alternative certificate subject name matches target host name`.

choices.text: The chain ends at the company's own CA, which the client's trust store lacks
choices.why: Nothing in the store signed anything in the chain: the message the office CA gave until it was installed.

choices.text: The certificate was signed by the server it identifies
choices.why: That one is `self-signed certificate`, verify code 18.

choices.text: The service runs from an image whose trust store holds no roots at all
choices.why: With an empty store nothing on the client signed anything in the chain, exactly as with an internal CA nobody installed.

prompt: A check from another region runs `curl -w` against the API every minute and prints `dns`, `tcp`, `tls`, `first byte` and `total`, each counted from the start. Match each reading to the suspect lesson 5 names for it.
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 5.

pairs.left: `dns` is large, and every step after it is small
pairs.right: the resolver

pairs.left: the step from `dns` to `tcp` is large
pairs.right: distance, or loss on the path

pairs.left: the step from `tcp` to `tls` is large, though `tcp` itself was quick
pairs.right: an overloaded server

pairs.left: the step from `tls` to `first byte` is large, and the rest quick
pairs.right: the application, still thinking

right_distractors: a firewall dropping the first packet

prompt: On a build server you ran `sudo usermod -aG docker bruno`, and `getent group docker` now lists him. In the ssh session he already had open, `docker ps` still answers `permission denied while trying to connect to the docker API at unix:///var/run/docker.sock`. What do you tell him?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 4; Docker and Containers, lesson 6.

choices.text: Restart the Docker daemon, so that it reads `/etc/group` again and admits him.
choices.why: The daemon is not the one holding a stale list. The socket checks the groups of the process that connects, and his shell still carries the list it started with.

choices.text: Run `sudo chmod 666 /var/run/docker.sock`, so the socket stops asking about groups.
choices.why: The socket controls a daemon that runs as root, so opening it to every account hands every account root on the machine, by another route.

choices.text: Log out and back in, or run `newgrp docker`: his shell still has its old groups.
choices.why: Group membership is attached to a process when it starts. The change is in `/etc/group`, and only a new login, or the new shell `newgrp` starts, picks it up.

choices.text: Run `sudo usermod -G docker bruno` instead; the `-a` kept the old groups in the way.
choices.why: Without `-a`, `-G` replaces every supplementary group he had, `sudo` included. And his open shell would still not see the change.

prompt: `docker stop` on one service takes exactly ten seconds every time. Its log never shows the shutdown message the program writes when it receives `SIGTERM`, and the container exits with `137`. The Dockerfile ends with `CMD shelf`. What is happening?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 6; Docker and Containers, lesson 11.

choices.text: Process 1 is `/bin/sh -c shelf`, which does not pass `SIGTERM` on; ten seconds later `SIGKILL` ends both.
choices.why: The shell form wraps the command in a shell, and the signal stops there. `SIGKILL` cannot be caught, so the program never logs or tidies up, and 128 plus 9 is 137. `CMD ["shelf"]` makes the program itself process 1.

choices.text: The program runs out of memory while it is shutting down, and 137 is the exit code that always means out of memory.
choices.why: 137 means killed by `SIGKILL`, whoever sent it. Docker records `OOMKilled=true` when it was memory, and a delay of exactly ten seconds is `docker stop` giving up.

choices.text: `docker stop` sends `SIGKILL` straight away rather than asking first, and 137 is what every stopped container reports.
choices.why: It sends `SIGTERM` first. The same program in exec form stopped in a fifth of a second and logged that it was shutting down.

choices.text: The program catches `SIGTERM` correctly and spends its ten seconds finishing the requests it still has open.
choices.why: A program that caught it would write its shutdown message and then exit with its own status. A status of 137 says it was killed, not that it finished.

prompt: `ssh` from your laptop to a new server hangs for a long while and ends with `Connection timed out`. On the server's console, `ss -tulpn` shows sshd in `LISTEN` on `0.0.0.0:22` with a `Recv-Q` of 0, and `systemctl is-active ssh` prints `active`. Where is the fault?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 11; Networks and Protocols, lesson 3.

choices.text: In sshd's configuration: it listens on the loopback address only, so nothing from outside reaches it.
choices.why: Loopback only would show `127.0.0.1:22`. `0.0.0.0` means every address on the machine, which is reachable from the network.

choices.text: In the listen backlog: it is full, so the kernel drops each new connection.
choices.why: On a listening socket a full backlog shows `Recv-Q` equal to `Send-Q`. A `Recv-Q` of 0 means nothing is waiting to be accepted.

choices.text: In sshd itself: a stopped service is what makes a connection time out.
choices.why: A port with nothing listening answers at once with `Connection refused`. And the service here is active and listening.

choices.text: Somewhere between the two machines: a firewall is discarding the attempt.
choices.why: The server side is up and listening on every address. No answer at all, after a long wait, is what a dropped packet looks like, so the question goes to whoever runs the firewall.

prompt: A nightly backup ran from root's crontab as `0 3 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1`, and the script exits non-zero on any failure. The server was rebuilt, came back with no crontab at all, and nobody noticed for three weeks. Which addition would have caught that?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 13; Observability and Operations, lesson 5.

choices.text: Drop the redirect from the line, so that cron mails each failure to the address in `MAILTO` instead.
choices.why: Cron mails what a job prints. A job that never starts prints nothing, so the mailbox stays as quiet as it does on a good night.

choices.text: Push the time of each successful run as a metric, and alert once it is more than a day plus some slack old.
choices.why: Now minus that time grows every second whether or not anything runs, so the alert fires on the night the job does not run. Of the four, it is the only check that does not need the job to start.

choices.text: Alert whenever the backup script exits with any status other than 0, as a failed run always does.
choices.why: A job that never ran has no exit status to alert on. This catches a run that failed, not a run that never happened.

choices.text: Wrap each run in a trace whose root span is named after the job, so every night leaves a record behind it.
choices.why: A trace exists only for work that happened. The night the scheduler is missing leaves no span at all.

prompt: On an Ubuntu server, an Nginx site says `root /home/ana/site;`. Every file under it is `-rw-r--r--`, and `/home/ana` is `drwxr-x---`, owned by `ana` with group `ana`. Every request for the site fails, and its error log reports a permission problem. What is wrong?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 4; Web Servers and Caching, lesson 1.

choices.text: The files need `x` for other as well as `r`, because Nginx executes the files that it serves to a client.
choices.why: `x` on a file means it may be run as a program. Nginx only reads them, and `r` for other is already there.

choices.text: Nothing about modes: the master process runs as root, and it reads every file itself before a worker sends it.
choices.why: The master reads the configuration and opens the port, and never answers a request. The workers do the serving.

choices.text: `www-data` needs `r` on `/home/ana`, because it has to list that directory before it can open a file inside it.
choices.why: `r` on a directory gives the list of names. Opening a file whose name you know needs `x` on the way, not `r`.

choices.text: The workers run as `www-data`, and other has no `x` on `/home/ana` to let them pass through.
choices.why: Every directory on the path needs `x` for the account asking. `namei -l` on the full path shows the one that stops it, whatever the files say.

prompt: A service started by systemd logs `Too many open files`. The on-call engineer runs `ulimit -n` in an ssh session, sees `20000`, raises it in that shell, and restarts the service with `systemctl restart`. Within the hour the error is back. Why did raising the limit change nothing?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 6.

choices.text: systemd sets the limit from `LimitNOFILE=` in the unit file; a login shell's setting never reaches it.
choices.why: A service does not get your shell's limits. And an error that comes back after a restart is usually a leak: `ls -l /proc/PID/fd | wc -l` counts the descriptors, and the list tends to name the culprit.

choices.text: `ulimit -n` limits how many processes an account may run, so it was the wrong limit to raise.
choices.why: `-n` is open files per process. The process limit is `ulimit -u`, a separate line in `ulimit -a`.

choices.text: Network connections live in a separate table of their own, which no open-files limit ever covers at all.
choices.why: Every network connection is a descriptor too, in the same table and counted against the same limit. That is why a busy server reaches it.

choices.text: A new open-files limit only takes effect after the whole machine reboots.
choices.why: It applies at once, to processes started from that shell. The service was started by systemd, so it was never one of them.

prompt: In a CI job, `./deploy.sh | grep -c ERROR` prints `0`, yet lines beginning with `ERROR` are plainly in the job's output just above it. What is happening?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 8.

choices.text: The pipe started `grep` before `deploy.sh` had written anything, so `grep` read an empty stream.
choices.why: Both stages run at once, and `grep` keeps reading whatever arrives until the stream ends. Timing is not the problem.

choices.text: The redirect belongs at the end of the line: `./deploy.sh | grep -c ERROR 2>&1`.
choices.why: That redirects `grep`'s own errors. Whatever `deploy.sh` writes to standard error still goes around the pipe.

choices.text: Those lines go to standard error, which a pipe does not carry, so `grep` never receives them.
choices.why: A pipe connects standard output only, and errors reach the screen by going around it. `./deploy.sh 2>&1 | grep -c ERROR` sends them into the pipe as well.

choices.text: `grep -c` counts occurrences rather than lines, and starts again from zero on each line.
choices.why: `-c` counts matching lines. Either way, lines that reached `grep` would never have counted as zero.

prompt: A colleague's unit file for a small API contains the lines below, and the service starts. Which of them will not do what they appear to?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 5.

choices.text: `RestartSec=5`
choices.why: It does what it says: wait five seconds before restarting, so a crash loop is not a tight one.

choices.text: `Restart=maybe`
choices.why: systemd fails to parse the value and drops the line, with `ignoring` in the message. The service will not restart on failure, and nothing says so unless you run `systemd-analyze verify`.

choices.text: `ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/api > /var/log/api.log`
choices.why: `ExecStart=` runs no shell, so `>` and the path arrive as two more arguments to the program. The output goes to the journal, not to that file.

choices.text: `User=api`
choices.why: It runs the service as that account, which is what the line says and what a service should do.

choices.text: `After=network.target`, so that the API can resolve its database's name when it starts
choices.why: `network.target` means the network is configured, not reachable. The honest version is `After=` and `Wants=` on `network-online.target`, with the `wait-online` service enabled.

choices.text: `Type=simple`, for a program that stays in the foreground
choices.why: That is exactly what `simple` is for. `forking` is the one that would go wrong here, with a start that hangs and times out.

prompt: Inside a container, `nproc` prints `8`, and its control group's `cpu.max` reads `150000 100000`. How many cores' worth of processor time can the container use?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 11.

prompt: On an Ubuntu server, `apt upgrade` has left the database package at the same old version for months and never mentioned it. Complete the command that lists every package somebody froze at its current version: `apt-mark ___`
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 7.

prompt: A second, empty disk has been attached to a server, and it must appear at `/data`, which already exists, on every boot from now on. Put the steps in order.
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 3.
items: `lsblk`, to find the new disk, which `df` cannot show while it is not mounted
`mkfs.ext4` on that device, to put a filesystem on it
`blkid`, to read the UUID the new filesystem was given
a line in `/etc/fstab` naming that UUID and `/data`
`sudo mount -a`, checking that it is silent before anybody reboots
trap: Writing `/etc/fstab` before `blkid` means naming the disk by its device letter, which changes when disks are added; the UUID only exists once `mkfs` has made the filesystem. And rebooting before `mount -a` turns a typo in `fstab` into a machine that does not boot.

prompt: Four scheduled jobs on an Ubuntu server misbehave. Match each symptom to its cause.
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 13.

pairs.left: `/etc/cron.d/backup.sh` has never run, and nothing anywhere complained
pairs.right: a dot in the file's name

pairs.left: cron's mail arrives with the subject `Cron <ana@vm> echo "ran at $(date +` and a shell syntax error
pairs.right: a percent sign the line did not escape

prompt: Production's Deployment uses `strategy: Recreate`, because the application migrates its database when it starts. A reviewed pull request moves production to `bulletin:1.9`, a tag nobody ever pushed; `validate.sh` passes it, and the production Kustomization has `wait: true` and `timeout: 2m`. What do production's users see, and what does Flux do?
hint: GitOps, Artefacts and Secrets, lesson 4; Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 35.

choices.text: The old version: the rollout keeps the old pods until a new one is ready.
choices.why: That is a rolling update holding back; `Recreate` removes every old pod before it creates any new one.

choices.text: The old version: two minutes later the health check fails and Flux applies the last revision that succeeded.
choices.why: `REVISION` names the last good commit as the one to return to; Flux does not go back by itself, and the fix is a revert.

choices.text: No page at all: the old pods go before the new ones fail to pull, and Flux reports a failed health check and undoes nothing.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: No change: Flux checks that the image exists in the registry before it applies the Deployment, and it stops at the missing tag.
choices.why: Nothing asks the registry first; a tag that was never pushed is a valid string, and the Deployment is applied.

prompt: The database's PersistentVolumeClaim `orders` uses a StorageClass whose `reclaimPolicy` is `Retain`. A pull request moves its files from `apps/shop/staging/`, which the Kustomization `staging` applies, to `infrastructure/db/`, which a new Kustomization `databases` applies; both have `prune: true`. After the merge, what does the database pod find on its disk?
hint: GitOps, Artefacts and Secrets, lesson 5; Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 26.

choices.text: Its data: a move in Git is not a delete in the cluster, so the claim stays where it was, adopted by `databases`.
choices.why: That holds while the same Kustomization keeps owning what moved; here `staging` prunes the claim and `databases` creates it again.

choices.text: An empty disk: the old claim was pruned, its volume sits `Released`, and the new claim got a new one.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Its data: with `Retain`, the claim that `databases` creates binds to the old volume, which still holds the rows.
choices.why: A `Released` volume still remembers its old claim and is not bound to a new one on its own; somebody has to clear `claimRef`.

choices.text: Its data: Flux refuses to apply `databases`, because the claim already belongs to the Kustomization `staging`.
choices.why: Flux has no such refusal here; the first Kustomization prunes what left its path and the second creates what arrived.

prompt: At three in the morning the person on call fixes an outage twice by hand and commits neither. One fix edits nginx's file on a VM whose Puppet agent runs with `runinterval = 1800`; the other changes a Deployment managed by an Argo CD Application with `selfHeal: true`. What happens to the two fixes?
hint: GitOps, Artefacts and Secrets, lesson 3; Infrastructure as Code, lesson 19.

choices.text: Both stay until the next merge, because an agent compares when its description changes.
choices.why: Both agents compare on their own: Puppet every half hour, and Argo CD whenever the objects it watches change.

choices.text: Argo CD reverts the Deployment on its next look at Git, up to three minutes later; Puppet keeps the edit until somebody runs it.
choices.why: The three-minute timer is for Git; `selfHeal` reacts to the cluster at once. And a Puppet agent runs on its timer, not when somebody remembers.

choices.text: Neither is reverted: an agent cannot tell a fix from a mistake, so it leaves alone what a person edited.
choices.why: It cannot tell them apart, which is exactly why it undoes both with the same confidence.

choices.text: The Deployment goes back within seconds, the nginx edit within half an hour, so a fix only lasts in the description.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: `bulletin:1.2` was signed with cosign by its digest, and production names that digest. A CI job is rerun on the same commit and pushes its rebuild as `bulletin:1.2` again. What does the course's `cosign verify` of `bulletin:1.2` report now, and what does production run?
hint: GitOps, Artefacts and Secrets, lesson 8; Docker and Containers, lesson 16.

choices.text: `no signatures found`: the new bytes have another digest, and the cluster keeps running the build that was signed.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Verified: the same commit and Dockerfile give the same digest, so the old signature still matches.
choices.why: Building the same commit again does not give the same image; its configuration records when it was built, so the digest differs.

choices.text: Verified, because the signature follows the tag `1.2` to wherever it points now.
choices.why: A signature covers a digest, never a tag; `cosign` resolves the tag and checks the digest it finds.

choices.text: `accepted signatures do not match threshold`, and production pulls the rebuild when its pods next start.
choices.why: That message means somebody else's signature exists; here there is none. And a reference by digest cannot follow a moved tag.

prompt: Eight months after staging went from two replicas to three, an auditor asks why. In a setup like this course's, which record holds the answer?
hint: GitOps, Artefacts and Secrets, lesson 12.

choices.text: Flux's events on the `staging` Kustomization, which name each revision it applied.
choices.why: They say which revision and when, never why, and they are kept for an hour by default.

choices.text: The pull request that made the change, with its description and its review.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The API server's audit log, which recorded the patch to the Deployment.
choices.why: It records who sent which request to which object; the reason was never part of the request.

choices.text: The Deployment's `managedFields`, which names the client that set `spec.replicas`.
choices.why: It names a client, not a person or a reason, and it keeps only the last writer of each field.

prompt: Production's ExternalSecret is changed to `refreshInterval: 15m`, and `bulletin` reads its token file on every request. Just after the operator's last read, a new token is put in Vault. Allowing for the kubelet's own sync, about how many minutes at most pass before the page shows the new fingerprint?
hint: GitOps, Artefacts and Secrets, lesson 10.

prompt: Publishing the chart to the course's registry, `helm push bulletin-0.1.0.tgz oci://localhost:5001/charts` fails with `server gave HTTP response to HTTPS client`. The registry runs on your own machine with no TLS, so the command needs one more flag: `--___`.
hint: GitOps, Artefacts and Secrets, lesson 7.

prompt: Pull request 3 moved staging to an image nobody built, the agent applied it, and `main` is protected. Put the way back in order.
hint: GitOps, Artefacts and Secrets, lesson 2; Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 4.
items: bring `main` up to date from the server and start a branch from it
`git revert -m 1` the merge commit, which adds a commit undoing it
push the branch and open a pull request
wait for the `validate` status and an approval from somebody else
merge, and let the agent apply the new `main` on its next pass
trap: The revert is a change like any other: it goes through the check and the review before the merge, and never straight onto `main`.

prompt: On a cluster moving from Argo CD to Flux, Argo CD's root Application manages the others. Put the switch in order, so that staging keeps running and only one agent ever applies its objects.
hint: GitOps, Artefacts and Secrets, lesson 4.
items: delete the root Application
delete the remaining Applications
delete Argo CD's own installation
install Flux and point it at `fleet`
trap: Deleting the other Applications before the root lets the root recreate them from `argocd/` on its next sync.

prompt: One bad morning with secrets produced four messages. Match each to what it means.
hint: GitOps, Artefacts and Secrets, lesson 9.

pairs.left: `ErrUnsealFailed` in a SealedSecret's events
pairs.right: a seal used under a name or namespace it was not made for

pairs.left: `Failed to get the data key` from `sops --decrypt`
pairs.right: nothing on this machine can open the file's data key

pairs.right: the store restarted and nobody has presented an unseal key

pairs.left: `service account name not authorized` at a Vault login
pairs.right: a genuine token from an account the role does not name

a file edited without SOPS, so its MAC no longer matches

prompt: A customer asks whether the fix in `bulletin` commit `a41c9e0` is live. In `bulletin`, `git tag --contains a41c9e0` prints `v1.3`. With Flux posting commit statuses to `fleet`, what completes the answer?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 12; GitOps, Artefacts and Secrets, lesson 12.

choices.text: That is enough: a tag in the application's repository marks a release, so 1.3 is what production runs today.
choices.why: The tag says which release contains the fix; in GitOps a release runs only once `fleet` names it.

choices.text: The image `bulletin:1.3` in the registry: once CI has pushed it there, production pulls it on its own.
choices.why: A registry is not a deployment; an image no directory names is run by nobody.

choices.text: A `kustomization/production` success status from Flux on a `fleet` commit whose production directory names 1.3.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The ticket's state: it closed by itself when the pull request carrying the fix was merged into `main`.
choices.why: A ticket closes on merge, before anybody outside the team can see the change; closed is not done.

prompt: The app reads a carrier token from `config.env`, which `.gitignore` keeps out of the repository. The contract test passes on Ana's laptop and fails in CI on the pull request, because the clean machine has no such file. What is the right fix?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 17; Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 9.

choices.text: Commit `config.env` as well, so that the clean machine CI creates has exactly what the laptop has.
choices.why: A secret that reaches a commit is leaked for good, in every clone and in the history.

choices.text: Add `!config.env` after the ignore rule, so that CI's clone brings the file while people keep their own copies.
choices.why: It is the same commit by another route: the token enters the history.

choices.text: Make the check optional on `main`, since what fails is the machine CI creates and not the code anybody wrote.
choices.why: A red check anybody can ignore gets ignored, and this failure is real: the code needs a value it does not have.

choices.text: Hand the token from CI's secrets to the one step that needs it, and have the program say when it is missing.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: At 15:00 on 21 September, Ana runs `git log --oneline --since=2026-09-17` to list everything from the 17th on. `31a6298 Add cheese rolls`, committed at 10:15 on the 17th, is not in the list. Why?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 3.

choices.text: A date with no time means that day at the current hour, 15:00, so the morning is cut off.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `--since` keeps only what came after the day it names, so the whole of the 17th is skipped.
choices.why: It keeps what happened from a moment on; what was misread is the moment, not the day.

choices.text: The commit is dated in UTC, and 10:15 at -03:00 already falls on the 16th by that clock.
choices.why: 10:15 at -03:00 is 13:15 UTC, the same day; the time zone is not what cut it.

choices.text: The date needed quotes, and without them Git ignores what follows the first of the hyphens.
choices.why: The shell passes `2026-09-17` whole; quotes only matter when the value has a space, as `2026-09-17 00:00` does.

prompt: On the team's board a card takes about two days from being started to being done, while the people who ask for something wait about five weeks for it. Where is the work waiting, and what is the question to ask?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 15.

choices.text: In review; lower the WIP limit on *in review* so that cards stop queuing there.
choices.why: Waiting in review would make cycle time long, and it is two days.

choices.text: In *to do*, before anybody starts it; that wait is about priorities or staffing.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: In progress; the tickets are too big and should be split before anybody starts them.
choices.why: Big tickets would also stretch the two days a card takes once it is started.

choices.text: Nowhere: lead time includes writing the ticket, so it dwarfs cycle time by design.
choices.why: Lead time does start when the ticket is written, but nothing makes five weeks normal; the gap is work waiting.

prompt: Bruno asks Ana to review a pull request of 1,900 lines before the end of the day, and she knows she cannot read it with care in that time. What should she do?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 13.

choices.text: Approve it once the checks are green, since a machine has already read the whole change.
choices.why: Checks catch what a script can; whether it does what the ticket asked needs somebody who read it.

choices.text: Comment on the names and the spacing, the part a quick read can cover.
choices.why: That spends the time on the last and least important of the four questions, which machines mostly cover.

choices.text: Say so plainly, and ask whether it can be split, or whether Bruno can walk her through it first.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Request changes on each file, so that the merge waits until she has time.
choices.why: That blocks the change with no reason anybody can act on; saying she cannot read it is the honest version.

prompt: Ana's branch is pushed, and Bruno has already pulled it. Which of these would give commits Bruno already has new ids? Choose all that apply.
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 6.

choices.text: `git commit --amend` on the last commit
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `git rebase main`, now that `main` has moved
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `git revert HEAD~1`, to undo a commit Bruno has
choices.why: Revert adds a new commit on top and leaves every existing one as it was.

choices.text: `git merge main` into the branch, to bring it up to date
choices.why: A merge adds a commit with two parents and rewrites nothing.

choices.text: `git rebase -i --autosquash HEAD~3`, with a `fixup!` in them
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `git push` of a new commit made on top of the branch
choices.why: A push only moves the branch forward; the commits Bruno has keep their ids.

prompt: A team of five finishes about 40 points in a normal ten-day sprint. This sprint two people have all ten days, one has six (a course), one has eight (two days on support) and one has six (a holiday). By lesson 18's arithmetic, about how many points is the team's capacity, before any slack is left?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 18.

prompt: The nightly backup runs as a Kubernetes CronJob, and each run is a pod that completes in about three seconds. The team wants to hear about any night the backup did not finish, including a night when no run started at all. Which arrangement tells them?
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 5; Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 12.

choices.text: Prometheus scrapes the backup pod's `/metrics` every fifteen seconds, and an alert fires when its success counter stops growing
choices.why: The pod is gone seconds after it starts, so a scrape every fifteen seconds rarely finds it, and a pod that never ran has nothing to scrape.

choices.text: An alert on the Job condition `BackoffLimitExceeded`, which Kubernetes sets on a run whose every retry has failed
choices.why: It catches a run that failed every retry. A night when the controller never created a Job leaves no Job and no condition to alert on.

choices.text: Each run pushes its finish time to a Pushgateway, and an alert fires once that time is 26 hours old
choices.why: The gap grows by a second every second whatever happens, so it fires on the night nothing runs, which no record of a run can do.

choices.text: Each run opens a root span named `nightly backup`, and the on-call engineer searches the trace store every morning
choices.why: A trace exists only for work that happened. The night the schedule failed leaves no span to find, and a morning search is a habit rather than an alert.

prompt: An API runs as a Deployment of 4 healthy replicas, each with a `readinessProbe` on `/ready` with `periodSeconds: 5` and a `livenessProbe` on `/healthz` with `periodSeconds: 10`. Its availability SLI counts every response that is not a `5xx`, on every route, as a good event. How many of the good events it counts each minute come from the kubelet rather than from customers?
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 15; Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 22.

prompt: A worker that exports its spans through the batch span processor keeps restarting. `docker inspect` gives its last exit code as 137, and Jaeger holds the traces of its older requests but none from the last few seconds before each restart. What explains the gap?
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 2; Linux and the Command Line, lesson 6.

choices.text: The bounded queue of 2048 spans overflowed under load and dropped the newest ones
choices.why: A full queue drops spans whenever the Collector stops answering, at any moment; it does not explain a gap that lines up with every death.

choices.text: 137 is 128 plus 9: `SIGKILL`, which cannot be caught, so the queued spans were never sent
choices.why: `SIGKILL` is very often the out-of-memory killer. A normal exit flushes the queue through the shutdown the SDK registered. A `KILL` gives the process no chance to run it, and the last seconds go with it.

choices.text: 137 is a clean exit after `SIGTERM`, so the spans were flushed and later dropped by the Collector
choices.why: `TERM` gives 143, not 137, and a process that handles it gets to empty its queue on the way out.

choices.text: The worker's traces are sampled, and its last seconds happened to fall among the dropped ones each time
choices.why: Sampling drops traces at random across the whole run, not in a block just before every restart.

prompt: Payments maintenance between 02:00 and 02:30 will make checkouts fail and trip the fast burn-rate page. The alert rules are manifests in Git, synced by Argo CD with `selfHeal: true`. At 01:55 the on-call engineer raises the rule's threshold with `kubectl edit`. What happens, and what was the right tool?
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 16; GitOps, Artefacts and Secrets, lesson 3.

choices.text: The edit holds until somebody pushes a new commit, so the page stays quiet; the engineer has to remember to undo it at 02:30
choices.why: `selfHeal` reacts to changes in the cluster, not only to commits, so the edit is undone within seconds.

choices.text: Argo CD reverts the edit; switching `selfHeal` off for the monitoring application during the work was the tool
choices.why: It gives up the guarantee for every other object in that application, and the switch outlives the maintenance unless somebody remembers it.

choices.text: The edit holds and the application shows OutOfSync; committing the higher threshold through a pull request was the tool
choices.why: Self-healing reverts the edit rather than reporting it, and a threshold raised in Git outlives the maintenance, which is what a silence avoids.

choices.text: Argo CD reverts it as drift in seconds and the page comes anyway; a silence with an end and a comment was the tool
choices.why: A silence lives in Alertmanager, outside what Argo CD reconciles, ends by itself at 02:30, and tells whoever finds the pager quiet who did it and why.

prompt: The catalogue API's latency SLI is computed from the shop's own request histogram: the share of requests answered within 500 ms. Nginx caches the API in front of the shop, with a hit ratio of 95 per cent. What does that SLI describe?
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 15; Web Servers and Caching, lesson 5.

choices.text: Only the one request in twenty that missed the cache, measured too far inside to see what customers got
choices.why: The shop never hears of a hit. The SLI judges the slowest twentieth of the traffic and nothing else, so it belongs at Nginx, nearer the customer.

choices.text: Every request a customer made, since Nginx passes each one to the shop through `proxy_pass`
choices.why: A hit is answered from Nginx's disk and no upstream is asked, which is why the cache log shows `upstream_time=-` for it.

choices.text: Every request, because Nginx checks each cached copy with the shop before it serves that copy to anybody
choices.why: That is a conditional request, used once a copy is stale. A fresh copy is served without asking anybody.

choices.text: Only the requests Nginx found in its cache, since a miss is Nginx refilling itself
choices.why: It is the other way round: a miss is exactly the request the shop sees.

prompt: Checkouts are failing, and the fast burn-rate page has just arrived, three minutes after a payments release. Put the response in the order lesson 17 runs it.
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 17.
items: Declare the incident where everybody can see it, naming the commander
Ask what changed, from the deploy marks of the last half hour
Roll back the release, and mark the rollback as it happens
Wait for the five-minute burn rate to fall below 1
Mark the incident resolved, with the follow-ups written down
Find the bug in the release that was rolled back
trap: Finding the bug before rolling back keeps customers failing while somebody reads code. The release is not lost, and understanding it is the postmortem's job once service is back.

prompt: A team's on-call channel is noisy. Match each source of noise to the fix lesson 16 pairs with it.
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 16.

pairs.left: alerts on causes that often heal themselves
pairs.right: page on the symptom, and turn the causes into tickets

pairs.left: one short blip, at any hour
pairs.right: require a high burn rate over a long window and a short one at once

pairs.left: one failure that sets off a hundred alerts
pairs.right: grouping in Alertmanager, and a page inhibiting its tickets

pairs.left: alerts during planned work
pairs.right: a silence with a reason and an end

right_distractors: raise each threshold until the alert stops firing
delete the rule for as long as the work lasts

prompt: The Collector holds every span of a trace until the trace is complete, then keeps every error, every slow request and 5% of the rest. Deciding there, once the request has ended, is called ___ sampling.
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 12.

prompt: A request counter is getting labels so that dashboards can break the traffic down. Which of these can it carry without the number of series growing with traffic?
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 6.

choices.text: the route's template, `/orders/{id}`
choices.why: One value per route the code defines, a handful however busy the shop gets.

choices.text: the id of the user who made the request
choices.why: One series per user: the experiment turned 3782 series into 43805 with this label.

choices.text: the HTTP method
choices.why: A few values at most, fixed by the protocol.

choices.text: the full URL, query string included
choices.why: Every distinct query string is a new value, and lesson 6 names it among the classic mistakes.

choices.text: the response's status code
choices.why: A short, known list, which is why lesson 5 could ask for every `5..` code at once.

choices.text: the order's id
choices.why: Every order becomes a series that lives on; the id belongs on the span or in the log line.

prompt: A product page calls a prices service, which takes 300 ms, and a stock service, which takes 140 ms, at the same moment, and answers when both have replied. A teammate spends a sprint bringing the stock call down to 40 ms. How much sooner does the page answer?
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 11.

choices.text: About 100 ms, since every millisecond cut from a span is cut from the request
choices.why: That holds only on the critical path. Here the request ends when the prices call does.

choices.text: About 50 ms, because two calls in parallel share any time one of them saves
choices.why: Parallel calls do not share a saving; the request waits for the slower one, whatever happens to the faster.

choices.text: Not noticeably: the page waits for prices, and stock had slack
choices.why: Stock finished 160 ms before prices even before the work. Shortening a span off the critical path shortens nothing.

choices.text: About 100 ms, provided stock was the span with the most self time
choices.why: Self time says who did the work, not what the request was waiting for, and the most self time can sit off the critical path.

prompt: The storefront samples traces with `parentbased_traceidratio` at `0.1`, and every other service follows its decision. Support pastes the trace id from the log line of a failed checkout into Jaeger and gets `trace not found`. What happened?
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 12.

choices.text: A service further down lost the context, so the storefront's id names a trace that never started
choices.why: A lost context splits a trace in two; it does not stop the storefront's own trace from existing.

choices.text: It was among the traces dropped at the root; its log line carries the id whatever the decision
choices.why: Head sampling decides before anything has happened, so a failed checkout is dropped as often as a fast one, and the formatter writes the id regardless.

choices.text: The formatter writes a trace id into a line when the trace is kept, so this id belongs to another request
choices.why: The id comes from the current span, recorded or not: every checkout in the lesson logged one, and none of the last ten was kept.

choices.text: Head sampling keeps every failed request, so the trace must still be waiting in the Collector
choices.why: That is what a tail policy on errors does. At the head nothing has failed yet when the decision is made.

prompt: The Collector sends every trace to Jaeger and, through a second exporter, to a hosted product's intake, at the lab's 35 spans a second. The intake stops answering for two hours. What happens to each copy?
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 13.

choices.text: Neither loses anything: the exporter keeps retrying until the intake is back, however long that takes
choices.why: Its queue holds 1000 batches, which at the lab's rate lasts about three quarters of an hour; after that it drops.

choices.text: Jaeger falls behind as well, because a pipeline waits for its slowest exporter
choices.why: Each exporter has its own queue and retries; in the lesson Jaeger kept receiving 35 spans a second while the other exporter sent none.

choices.text: Jaeger loses nothing; the hosted copy queues for about three quarters of an hour, then drops spans
choices.why: Each destination fails alone. The queue is memory with room for 1000 batches, so the outage it can ride out is a decision about its size.

choices.text: Both copies lose spans, since the Collector drops any batch that one of its destinations refuses
choices.why: A refusal stays with the exporter that met it. The other destinations never see it.

prompt: To find a checkout's log lines faster, a colleague proposes turning each line's `trace_id` field into a Loki label. What would that do?
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 9.

choices.text: Nothing, because Loki already indexes every field of every line it stores
choices.why: That is Elasticsearch's choice. Loki indexes the labels of each stream and reads the lines when asked.

choices.text: Speed lookups up at no cost, because labels are compressed along with the chunks
choices.why: The chunks are compressed; the labels are the index, and every new value adds to it.

choices.text: Be refused, because Loki allows the service name as a stream's one label
choices.why: The lab has one label because the Collector made one. Loki takes others, which is why the advice is about which values belong there.

choices.text: Make every trace id its own stream, so Loki's index grows with traffic
choices.why: A label per request is a stream per value. The id belongs in the line, where a line filter or `| json` finds it.

prompt: A product manager asks for an objective of 99.99% of checkouts succeeding over 28 days. Being paged, reading the alert and opening a laptop takes the on-call engineer about ten minutes. What is wrong with the objective?
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 15.

choices.text: The window: 28 days counts a Monday rush twice against some months
choices.why: Twenty-eight days is chosen because it holds four of each weekday, so no rush is counted twice.

choices.text: It allows about 4 minutes of outage in 28 days, less than the response itself takes
choices.why: Each nine is a factor of ten, and the fourth leaves less time than it takes to notice. An objective tighter than the team can respond to is a promise nobody can keep.

choices.text: It is too loose, since customers notice failures long before the fourth nine
choices.why: The reverse: a customer cannot tell 99.99% from 100%, because their own phone and network fail more often than that.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the contract's SLA states the same 99.99%
choices.why: An SLA is kept looser than the SLO so that the team hears about trouble from its own objective first; equal numbers remove that warning.

prompt: To raise the edge's hit ratio, the stylesheets and images move to `static.ipelivros.example`, behind the same Varnish, so that their requests carry no cookies. That host's hit ratio stays near zero. The analytics script on `www.ipelivros.example` sets its cookie with `Domain=ipelivros.example`. Why?
hint: Web Servers and Caching, lesson 7; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 7.

choices.text: That attribute sends the cookie to every subdomain, `static.` included, and Varnish passes any request carrying a `Cookie`
choices.why: Widening the cookie undid the move. Leave `Domain` out so it returns only to the host that set it, or remove cookies at the edge for the assets.

choices.text: A cookie set by a script stays with the host that set it, so the misses come from `utm_` parameters on the asset links
choices.why: Who set it does not matter; the `Domain` attribute decides where it goes. And the lab's VCL already strips `utm_` before the key is made.

choices.text: Varnish's built-in logic passes static files to the origin, cookie or not, until the VCL says otherwise
choices.why: The built-in logic stores public responses of any type; it passes a request because of its `Cookie` or `Authorization`, not its file type.

choices.text: A cookie for the parent domain is third-party on `static.`, so the browser blocks it and the edge cannot recognise the visitor
choices.why: Third-party means set by something embedded from another site. This cookie is the site's own, and the browser sends it.

prompt: An old landing page still has a newsletter form that posts to `http://ipelivros.example/api/subscribe`. Since the port-80 block began answering `return 301 https://$host$request_uri;`, no subscription arrives, and the shop logs `GET /api/subscribe` with no body. What should that block answer instead?
hint: Web Servers and Caching, lesson 3; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6.

choices.text: `308`, which tells the browser to repeat the request with the same method and body
choices.why: `308` is the permanent redirect that keeps the method, the meaning `301` was meant to have. Caddy answered HTTP with it in the same lesson.

choices.text: `302`, so that browsers do not remember the move while it is being tested
choices.why: A `302` is not remembered, and it has the same history as `301`: browsers turn the `POST` into a `GET`.

choices.text: `303`, which sends the browser to the HTTPS address of the same path
choices.why: `303` turns the request into a `GET` on purpose; it is for the page after a form, not for the form itself.

choices.text: The same `301` with `Strict-Transport-Security` added, so that the browser goes to HTTPS before it posts
choices.why: A browser ignores HSTS received over plain HTTP, which is why the site sends it on 443 alone.

prompt: With the catch-all block in place, `curl -k https://<the server's IP>/` fails with `tlsv1 unrecognized name`, and no certificate ever reaches the client. How does Nginx pick the catch-all block before the client has sent a `Host` header?
hint: Web Servers and Caching, lesson 4; Networks and Protocols, lesson 5.

choices.text: The client's certificate, sent first in the handshake, names the site it wants
choices.why: An ordinary browser or `curl` sends no certificate at all; the server is the side that proves its name.

choices.text: Nginx reads the request's `Host` header first, and only then decides whether to finish the handshake
choices.why: The request travels after the handshake, encrypted. Nginx has to choose before it holds any key to read it with.

choices.text: Each site on the machine has its own IP address, so the address chooses the block
choices.why: One address serves every site here; that is why Nginx needs the name at all.

choices.text: The wanted name rides in the Client hello as SNI, readable before any key exists, and a bare IP gives no name to match
choices.why: The server needs the name to pick a certificate, so it arrives in the clear. `ssl_reject_handshake` refuses right there, and no `server_name` matches an address.

prompt: `shop@2` crashes and stays down. The upstream lists both copies with default settings, the catalogue API serves only `GET`s, and the one paging alert is a burn-rate alert on the share of `5xx` answers Nginx gives. What does the next hour look like?
hint: Web Servers and Caching, lesson 2; Observability and Operations, lesson 16.

choices.text: A page every ten seconds or so, each time `fail_timeout` lets one real request through to the dead copy
choices.why: That request is refused and Nginx tries it again on `shop1` before the client notices, so it ends as a `200`.

choices.text: No page, and rightly: customers see no errors, and the dead copy should surface as a ticket, such as one on `up == 0`
choices.why: Nginx's retry turns every refused connection into an answer from `shop1`. The symptom is absent, so the cause belongs to working hours.

choices.text: A page at once: half the upstream is gone, and with it half the capacity
choices.why: The alert watches what customers receive, and they receive `200`s. A missing copy is a cause, and causes are tickets.

choices.text: No page, which is a gap: a page on `shop2`'s own error ratio has to be added
choices.why: A copy that refuses connections reports no ratio at all, and paging on causes is the noise lesson 16 removes.

prompt: A bestseller's page is read 800 times a second, and the database query that rebuilds its cached copy takes 150 milliseconds. With plain cache-aside and no protection, about how many identical queries reach the database when its key expires?
hint: Web Servers and Caching, lesson 11.

prompt: Each copy of an application keeps a visitor's half-filled basket in its own memory, so the upstream uses `hash $remote_addr` to send each client to the same copy every time. That arrangement is called session ___.
hint: Web Servers and Caching, lesson 2.

prompt: A team runs Redis in four places. Match each use to the `maxmemory-policy` it should run with.
hint: Web Servers and Caching, lesson 8.

pairs.left: the one copy of a queue of orders waiting to be processed
pairs.right: `noeviction`

pairs.left: a cache where any key may go to make room
pairs.right: `allkeys-lru`

pairs.left: a cache whose popular keys stay the same week after week
pairs.right: `allkeys-lfu`

pairs.left: one instance holding cache keys with a lifetime beside data keys without one
pairs.right: `volatile-lru`

prompt: Nginx caches the shop's API with `proxy_cache` and its default settings. Which of these responses will it store and hand to the next visitor who asks?
hint: Web Servers and Caching, lesson 5.

choices.text: an account page sent with `Cache-Control: private, max-age=60`
choices.why: `private` keeps it out of every shared cache; three requests in the lesson gave three `MISS`es.

choices.text: a catalogue listing sent with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60`
choices.why: Public, with a lifetime: exactly what a shared cache is for.

choices.text: a basket sent with `Cache-Control: no-store`
choices.why: `no-store` forbids storing it anywhere at all.

choices.text: a book sent with `Cache-Control: max-age=60`
choices.why: Nginx took its lifetime from this header in the lesson: `MISS`, then `HIT`, `HIT`.

choices.text: a book sent with `Cache-Control: max-age=60` and a `Set-Cookie` header
choices.why: Nginx refuses on its own to store a response that sets a cookie.

prompt: A self-run control plane keeps etcd on seven members, which agree on every write by a majority. How many members can fail at the same time while etcd still accepts writes?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 47.

prompt: Ana changes `GREETING` in the base's `configMapGenerator` and runs `kubectl apply -k deploy/overlays/production`. Put what follows in order, until the new greeting reaches the pods.
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 38.
items: Kustomize renders a ConfigMap whose name carries a new hash of its contents
the new ConfigMap is created, and the old one is left where it was
the Deployment's pod template now names the new ConfigMap
the Deployment makes a new ReplicaSet for the changed template
new pods start with the new `GREETING` in their environment
trap: Running pods never see a variable change in a ConfigMap; the greeting arrives only because the new name changes the template, and a changed template is a rollout.

prompt: A customer's request reaches the shop through a Service of type LoadBalancer. Put the places it passes through in order, from the outside in.
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 15.
items: the provider's balancer, at the Service's `EXTERNAL-IP` on port 80
the Service's NodePort on one of the nodes
the rules kube-proxy wrote into that node's kernel, which pick one pod
port 8080 of the chosen pod, the Service's `targetPort`
trap: The balancer does not send to pods: a LoadBalancer is a NodePort with a machine in front of it, and the pod is chosen on the node.

prompt: A team reads the VerticalPodAutoscaler's recommendations for a month before trusting it. Match each `updateMode` with what the VPA then does to the pods.
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 34.

pairs.left: `Off`
pairs.right: recommends requests and changes no pod

pairs.left: `Initial`
pairs.right: writes its requests into new pods and never touches running ones

pairs.left: `Recreate`
pairs.right: evicts pods so that their replacements start with new requests

pairs.left: `InPlaceOrRecreate`
pairs.right: resizes pods in place where it can, and evicts them where it cannot

right_distractors: adds replicas when the average use passes a target

prompt: A pipeline's Role grants `get`, `list` and `watch` on `pods`, yet its request for what a container printed is refused. The Role also has to name the subresource `pods/___`.
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 23.

prompt: The release `shop` runs `shop:1.1` with three copies, yet the chart's `values.yaml` says tag `1.0` and two replicas. A colleague concludes that the chart is broken. Which command answers first, and what will it show?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 37.

choices.text: `helm history shop`, whose list of revisions records the values each upgrade set.
choices.why: It lists revisions with their status and chart version; the values somebody supplied are not in it.

choices.text: `helm get values shop`, listing only what was supplied at install or upgrade.
choices.why: It shows the overrides, such as `--set image.tag=1.1`, and leaves the defaults out, which is why it is the first check for a release that differs from its chart.

choices.text: `helm template shop shop-chart`, which prints what the cluster is running now.
choices.why: It renders the chart with its defaults and touches no cluster; without the overrides it would show tag `1.0`.

choices.text: `helm lint shop-chart`, since a chart that renders the wrong values fails lint.
choices.why: Lint checks that the chart renders and follows the conventions; a release's values are unknown to it.

prompt: A CronJob runs a backup at `0 2 * * *`, with `timeZone` set. The control plane is upgraded from 01:50 to 02:20, so the controller manager is not running at 02:00. What happens to that night's backup?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 12.

choices.text: It runs at 02:00 anyway, because the kubelet on a worker node keeps the CronJob's schedule.
choices.why: The schedule belongs to the CronJob controller, inside the controller manager; a kubelet only runs pods it is given.

choices.text: It is skipped until the next night, because a schedule fires on its own minute or not at all.
choices.why: A run that was due while the controller was down is started when it comes back, unless a deadline says it is too late.

choices.text: It runs twice after 02:20: once for the minute it missed, once to catch up.
choices.why: The missed run is started once; nothing in the lesson makes a second one.

choices.text: It starts once the controller is back, unless `startingDeadlineSeconds` is shorter.
choices.why: Lesson 12's rule: a run that was due while the controller was down starts late, and only `startingDeadlineSeconds` can declare it too late.

prompt: The cluster autoscaler keeps more nodes on the bill than the workload seems to need. By lesson 34, which of these can be the reason? Choose all that apply.
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 34.

choices.text: Requests far above what the pods use, since a node is added when requests do not fit
choices.why: It buys machines for requests, never for usage, so the waste of lesson 21 turns into nodes.

choices.text: Pods that use more CPU than they request, which the autoscaler counts as demand
choices.why: Usage is not what it reads: it adds a node for pods that are `Pending` for lack of room.

choices.text: A PodDisruptionBudget that allows no disruption to a pod on that node
choices.why: Removing a node drains it, and a pod it may not move keeps the whole machine alive.

choices.text: metrics-server keeping only the newest sample, so the quiet hours are forgotten
choices.why: The cluster autoscaler decides from pending pods and from pods that fit elsewhere, not from a history of metrics.

choices.text: A pod annotated as not safe to evict, which the autoscaler is not allowed to move
choices.why: The `safe-to-evict` annotation is the other thing lesson 34 names: one such pod can keep a node on the bill.

choices.text: A VerticalPodAutoscaler with `updateMode: "Off"` beside the Deployment
choices.why: `Off` only recommends; it changes no request, so it changes no node either.

prompt: Under Docker, `shelf` ran with `--memory 64m --cpus 0.5`. Moved to Kubernetes, its manifest says `resources.requests: {cpu: 500m, memory: 64Mi}` and has no `limits`. A leak makes the process grow past 300 MiB. What happens at 64 MiB?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 19; Docker and Containers, lesson 17.

choices.text: Nothing: a request reserves room for the scheduler; only a limit is an enforced ceiling.
choices.why: Docker's `--memory` and `--cpus` are cgroup limits; in a manifest that is `limits`, while `requests` is a reservation nobody measures usage against.

choices.text: The kernel kills it with `OOMKilled`, as Docker did, since a request sets the same cgroup ceiling.
choices.why: Only a limit is handed to the kernel as a cgroup ceiling; a request is arithmetic for the scheduler.

choices.text: The kubelet throttles its memory at 64 MiB, the way a CPU limit slows a container.
choices.why: Memory cannot be paused and given back; at a memory limit the container dies, and here there is no limit at all.

choices.text: The scheduler moves the pod to another node that has more free memory.
choices.why: The scheduler places a pod once and never moves a running one.

prompt: The `db` Secret is the one piece of the shop that is not yet in the GitOps repository. A colleague proposes committing its manifest as `kubectl get secret db -o yaml` prints it: "the values are base64, and the repository is private". What do the lessons say?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 14; GitOps, Artefacts and Secrets, lesson 9.

choices.text: No: leave it out of Git and create the Secret by hand with `kubectl create secret` on each cluster.
choices.why: Then the cluster holds a piece of state nobody reviewed, nobody versioned and nobody can rebuild, which is the other way a secret breaks the rule.

choices.text: Commit it, because only the people who already run the cluster can read a private repository.
choices.why: A repository is copied to every laptop that clones it, and to every backup, and keeps the value in its history for good.

choices.text: No: one command undoes base64. Commit a copy encrypted with Sealed Secrets or SOPS, or a reference to an entry in Vault.
choices.why: Those are the lesson's three answers: an encrypted copy in Git, or a reference in Git with the value kept in a store.

choices.text: Commit it, as long as the cluster has encryption at rest turned on for Secrets, so that the stored values are ciphertext.
choices.why: Encryption at rest protects etcd's copy of the data and does nothing for the copy in Git.

prompt: Under `kubectl apply -k`, every change to the base's greeting left one more `shop-settings-<hash>` ConfigMap behind in `production`. The team puts the overlay under Argo CD with automated sync and `prune: true`. What changes, and what risk comes with it?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 38; GitOps, Artefacts and Secrets, lesson 3.

choices.text: Nothing changes for the ConfigMaps, because prune acts on whole namespaces and not on the objects in them.
choices.why: Prune deletes any object it tracks that the rendered manifests no longer contain, ConfigMaps included.

choices.text: The stale ConfigMaps are deleted, and so is anything deleted from Git by mistake.
choices.why: That is prune: the cluster follows Git in removals too, so a file deleted by mistake becomes an object deleted on the next sync.

choices.text: Argo CD stops adding the hash, so a new greeting edits one ConfigMap in place.
choices.why: The hash comes from Kustomize's generator, and it is what makes a changed setting roll out new pods.

choices.text: The ConfigMaps stay where they are, because Argo CD prunes just the objects that came from a Helm chart.
choices.why: Argo CD renders plain manifests, Kustomize and Helm alike, and prunes whatever it tracks.

prompt: The front end's readiness probe calls the shop's `/ready`, and the shop's `/ready` checks the database. The database stops for two minutes. What do the probes do, and what is wrong with the design?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 22; Observability and Operations, lesson 14.

choices.text: The shop pods leave their Service and the front end stays in, because readiness is judged separately for each pod.
choices.why: The front end's own probe gets the shop's 503, so the front-end pods fail readiness as well.

choices.text: Both sets of pods are restarted every few seconds until the database comes back.
choices.why: A readiness failure takes a pod out of its Service and restarts nothing; restarting is liveness.

choices.text: The shop's containers restart once their readiness probe passes its `failureThreshold`.
choices.why: Readiness has no restart; `failureThreshold` only decides when the pod leaves the endpoints.

choices.text: Both leave their Services, pages without the database included; check only your own dependencies.
choices.why: The first rule of a readiness check: test what this service needs, never another service's readiness, or one outage spreads to everything that asks.

prompt: At three in the morning a `shop` pod was evicted from its node and replaced by a new one. In the morning, `kubectl logs` with the old pod's name finds nothing, although the shop prints every request to standard output. What do the lessons put in place so that lines like these outlive their pod?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 41; Observability and Operations, lesson 9.
